analysis.title: The risks reshaping global AI investment (UBS House View - Daily Asia)
key_insights: NVIDIA shares fell more than 4.3% on Thursday (11/12), helping pull the Nasdaq down around 0.4% and pressuring tech-heavy Taiwan and South Korea markets, after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following reports he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
NVIDIA named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, started a permanent CEO search and appointed Harvey C. Jones as board chair.
UBS says tech volatility reflects a shift from rewarding spending commitments toward assessing monetization, balance sheet strength, capacity utilization and prospective returns.

Underlying AI demand remains robust: recent earnings showed accelerating cloud revenue and expanding orders for computing capacity. UBS forecasts aggregate AI capex of USD 1.0tr in 2026 and USD 1.4tr in 2027.

Key-person risk deserves more attention. Leadership and governance can become material investment factors when a company's strategy and standing are tied to one individual, especially after AI equity gains concentrated in a narrow group of companies. Succession planning may matter more alongside earnings growth.
UBS believes the developments reduce the likelihood of easing current restrictions on advanced AI-chip shipments to China, and scrutiny of where processors are ultimately deployed could increase.
Tighter restrictions could weigh on sales in some overseas markets but would not necessarily change underlying AI demand, since compute capacity remains in short supply.

AI is increasingly a geopolitical issue. Possible results include tracking requirements, regulatory scrutiny, higher costs and restricted access in some overseas markets, plus more investment in alternative supply chains and domestic AI capacity.

Positioning: UBS keeps conviction in the structural AI opportunity but argues for more selectivity and diversification. It favors financially strong hyperscalers, since tighter compute capacity could raise the value of existing infrastructure and lower capex could support free cash flow.

Within AI picks and shovels (semiconductors and hardware), UBS stays selective and favors quality companies with less margin expansion to unwind, plus defensive tech such as payment networks and potential beneficiaries of lower memory costs within consumer electronics.
For investors with overly concentrated tech exposure, UBS would consider broadening within technology and diversifying across sectors, asset classes and geographies.
Data to watch 13 November: US producer prices report, Fed speeches including Vice Chair Michelle Bowman and SF Fed President Mary Daly, and EU Q3 2026 GDP.

Defensive technology exposures, and consumer electronics could benefit from lower memory costs.

vol_and_positioning: Tech volatility reflects a shift from rewarding spending commitments to assessing monetization, balance sheet strength, capacity utilization and returns.

AI equity gains have been concentrated in a relatively narrow group of businesses, and UBS suggests broadening exposure within technology and diversifying across sectors, asset classes and geographies.
geopolitical: Reports that NVIDIA's CEO was the target of a foreign intelligence effort
US-China AI competition under tight restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports, with easing now seen as less likely
Possible greater tracking of chip deployment and regulatory scrutiny of global AI supply chains
Possible investment in alternative supply chains and domestic AI capacity
